title: No d Electrons, Still Purple: Why KMnO₄ Is So Intensely Coloured
subject: Chemistry
objective: In MnO₄⁻ manganese is +7 (3d⁰), so no d–d transition is possible. The colour comes from ligand-to-metal charge transfer: visible light moves an electron from an oxygen into the empty d orbitals of Mn. This absorbs green-yellow light (≈ 525 nm), so the solution looks purple. Charge transfer is an allowed transition, so it absorbs far more light than restricted d–d transitions: KMnO₄ is intensely coloured while Ti³⁺(aq) or Mn²⁺(aq) are pale. Chromate (yellow) and dichromate (orange), also d⁰, are coloured the same way.

num.q: Find the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO₄.
Find the oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ and its d-electron count.

short.solution: Mn is +7 (3d⁰), so no d–d transition. Visible light (green-yellow, ≈ 525 nm) moves an electron from oxygen to the empty d orbitals of Mn (ligand-to-metal charge transfer); the remaining red + blue light looks purple.
Charge-transfer transitions are allowed, whereas d–d transitions are restricted by symmetry (Laporte rule), so many more photons are absorbed in charge transfer.

short.q: Name two ions other than MnO₄⁻ coloured by charge transfer.
short.solution: CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) and Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange); both contain Cr(VI), d⁰, with O → Cr charge transfer.

right: d⁰, purple, O → Mn charge transfer
